title: Reading the screen
lede: Everything else in this series builds a concept. This page is about a screen — the grid of strikes and expiries a trader looks at several hundred times a day — and the small conversions that turn it from a wall of numbers into a picture. It is the most practical page here and the least theoretical, and it assumes you have met delta and implied volatility somewhere before.
claims: $100 at 30 vol, 30 days: one sigma is $8.60

the band grows roughly linearly in the width

the exact answer is always accepted
an answer well outside the band is rejected
the 85 call is below the screen's parity bound

in-the-money put carries more delta than the out-of-the-money call
and annual vol / 16 is the daily move

chapters.title: A chain is a distribution printed sideways
chapters.dek: The column of prices down a single expiry is a probability distribution. Once you can see that, the screen stops being a list.

figures.title: The same column, as a table and as the density it is
figures.caption: Notice the table and the curve carry identical information. One of them can be read in a glance and the other cannot, and the screen only ever gives you the second.

checks.q: Why is reading a chain row by row the wrong default?
checks.right: Because the information is in the shape across strikes, not in any single row. A row tells you one price; the column tells you what the market thinks the distribution is
checks.why: The information lives across the column, not down it. Slowness is a symptom. The real cost is that a single row cannot tell you whether a price is high or low — that judgement is always relative to its neighbors, and the neighbors are what the eye is for.

chapters.text: Open any chain and the first instinct is to read it like a table — find the strike you care about, read its row, move on. That is the slow way, and it is the way that misses everything. Page 07 established that the second derivative of call price across strikes is the risk-neutral density. Which means the column you are looking at is a distribution, drawn in a coordinate system nobody would have chosen. Every skill on this page is a way of undoing that coordinate system fast enough to be useful. Three conversions do almost all of it. Turn dollars into sigmas, so strikes on a $30 stock and a $600 stock are comparable. Turn prices into deltas, so moneyness is comparable across expiries. And turn the IV column into a shape rather than a list of numbers — a slope and a curvature, which is what your eye is good at and what arithmetic is slow at. The same column, as a table and as the density it is Controls Notice the table and the curve carry identical information. One of them can be read in a glance and the other cannot, and the screen only ever gives you the second.

chapters.title: A strike's distance in dollars is meaningless
chapters.dek: Five points away is 2.33 standard deviations on one stock and 0.12 on another. The conversion is one multiplication and it is the most valuable habit on this page.

figures.title: How many strikes fit inside one standard deviation
figures.caption: Notice how fast this falls at the short end. Below the red line there is not even one strike inside the expected move, and a spread built there is quantized far more coarsely than its price suggests.

figures.title: Find one sigma, against the clock
figures.caption: The first chain is a $90.21 stock with 45 days to run at 43.4% vol, listed every $2.50: one sigma is $13.75, five and a half strikes, and the answer is the 105 call. The next chain may put one sigma less than a strike away. The tick marks under the curve are the listed strikes; the distance between them means nothing until it is measured in sigmas.

checks.q: A $40 stock at 45 volatility, weekly expiry, 2.5-point strikes. Roughly how far apart are the strikes in sigmas?
checks.right: About 1 sigma. One sigma is 40 × 0.45 × √(7/365) = $2.49, so the 2.5-point spacing is essentially the whole expected move
checks.why: About one sigma per strike. Which tells you immediately that there are perhaps three strikes worth quoting in that expiry, that a one-strike-wide spread there is a very different animal from a one-strike-wide spread on an index, and that the delta will move in large jumps as you walk down the column. All from one multiplication done before you looked at any prices.

chapters.text: Every chain is laid out in dollars, and dollars are the one unit that does not travel. Take four stocks at 30 volatility with thirty days to expiry, all with five-point strike spacing, and ask how far apart the strikes really are. On a $25 stock, one standard deviation is $2.15, so consecutive strikes are 2.33 sigma apart — you get less than half a strike inside the entire expected move, and the chain is hopelessly coarse. On a $500 stock the same five points is 0.12 sigma and there are 8.6 strikes inside one standard deviation. Same spacing on the screen; completely different instruments. The conversion is this, and it should become automatic: [equation: one sigma = S · σ · √T z = (K − S) / (S · σ · √T)] Reads as: multiply the spot by the volatility by the square root of the time, and you have the dollar size of a one-standard-deviation move. Divide any strike's distance by it and you have a number that means the same thing on every name on the screen. The mental shortcut worth carrying is √T for the common tenors: a month is about 0.29, a quarter about 0.5, a year is 1. So a $100 stock at 30 vol has a one-sigma move of about $8.60 over a month, $15 over a quarter and $30 over a year. Those three numbers, held in the head, convert most of a screen without a calculator. The same arithmetic run across expiries is where the intuition really lands. On one stock with one strike spacing, consecutive strikes are 3.18 sigma apart on a one-day option and 0.17 sigma apart on a one-year one. A weekly chain is a blunt instrument by construction, and that has nothing to do with liquidity — it is geometry. How many strikes fit inside one standard deviation Controls Notice how fast this falls at the short end. Below the red line there is not even one strike inside the expected move, and a spread built there is quantized far more coarsely than its price suggests. Now do it at the speed the job wants. Each rep puts a different chain in front of you, any price from $20 to $500, any expiry, any vol. Click the call strike one standard deviation above spot. The rule is the one above, S × σ × √T, done in your head; the clock is running. Find one sigma, against the clock The chain The first chain is a $90.21 stock with 45 days to run at 43.4% vol, listed every $2.50: one sigma is $13.75, five and a half strikes, and the answer is the 105 call. The next chain may put one sigma less than a strike away. The tick marks under the curve are the listed strikes; the distance between them means nothing until it is measured in sigmas. Trader's lens Before anything else on a chain, a trader converts the strikes into sigmas, because every other judgement, cheap or rich, near or far, hedge or not, depends on it. The arithmetic is done in the head in a few seconds, with round numbers, and checked against the deltas on the screen. Daily sigma ≈ annual vol ÷ 16, so a 32-vol stock moves about 2% a day. The roughly 16-delta call sits near one sigma out; the screen gives you a free check. Scale by √T: four times the time is twice the move. Rule of thumb: one sigma to expiry ≈ price × vol × √(days ÷ 365); for 30 days, √(30/365) ≈ 0.29. Try this Set the spot to 25 and predict how many strikes fit inside a one-sigma move on the monthly. Then set it to 500 and see the same screen become a different instrument.

chapters.title: Delta is the ruler, and the rule of thumb has a shelf life
chapters.dek: The 16-delta option is roughly a one-sigma strike. Roughly holds for about three months, and the put side was never symmetric with the call side.

figures.title: Where each delta actually sits, in standard deviations
figures.caption: Notice the two curves are not mirror images and the gap widens with time. That asymmetry is the lognormal, and it is the reason delta-defined structures drift as they age.

checks.q: Someone asks for "the 25-delta call" on a one-year chain. How far out is that?
checks.right: About 1.11 sigma on the year, against 0.78 on the month. Delta is comparable across expiries as a label but not as a distance
checks.why: A delta names a strike, not a distance. That is exactly why desks quote in deltas — a 25-delta option has roughly comparable character across expiries even though it sits at very different moneyness. Trouble only starts when someone treats the delta as if it were a fixed number of standard deviations, which is the mistake this chapter exists to prevent.

chapters.text: The second conversion is easier because the screen does it for you. Delta is printed, it runs from zero to one on every name and every expiry, and it is the closest thing a chain has to a universal coordinate. The rule everyone half-knows is that a 16-delta option is about a one-sigma strike , because 16% is the tail beyond one standard deviation of a normal. It is a good rule and it is worth knowing exactly how good. On a $100 stock at 30 volatility the 16-delta call sits at 1.06 sigma at a week, 1.13 sigma at a month and 1.24 sigma at three months — so inside a quarter it is accurate to about a tenth of a sigma, which is fine. At a year it is 1.56 sigma and the rule has stopped being useful. The part almost nobody mentions is the asymmetry. Over the same tenors the 16-delta put sits at 0.94 , 0.88 , 0.80 and 0.64 sigma — it moves the other way. The lognormal is not symmetric, so equal deltas are not equal distances, and a "16-delta strangle" is not centered on anything. One more, because it catches people constantly: the at-the-money call's delta is 0.53 here, not 0.50. Scanning a column for the 50-delta to find the money will put you a strike above it, because delta falls as the strike rises. Where each delta actually sits, in standard deviations Controls Notice the two curves are not mirror images and the gap widens with time. That asymmetry is the lognormal, and it is the reason delta-defined structures drift as they age. Try this Drag the expiry out to a year and watch the rule of thumb fail. Predict first whether the call or the put drifts further.

chapters.title: What each column is actually telling you
chapters.dek: The IV column is a single number chosen out of a range, and the width of that range is the bid-offer.

figures.title: The volatility band a quote actually implies
figures.caption: Notice the band widens sharply out in the wings even at constant quote width. The same ten cents is a fifth of a point at the money and several points on a far strike, because vega collapses faster than the spread does.

checks.q: Two names both show 32.4% implied on the at-the-money. One is quoted a penny wide, the other twenty cents. What can you conclude?
checks.right: Almost nothing about the second one. Twenty cents on an at-the-money is roughly a two-point volatility band, so "32.4%" there means somewhere between about 31.4 and 33.4
checks.why: The number is only as good as the spread behind it. The fourth answer is the tempting one and it is exactly backwards: illiquidity does not merely make a market harder to trade, it makes the derived quantities imprecise, because they are computed from a midpoint that is a guess. Any screen comparison across names should carry the spread alongside the implied, and most do not.

chapters.text: A chain prints a lot of columns and they are not equally trustworthy. The one that misleads most is the one that looks most authoritative. Implied volatility is computed from a price, and the screen has at least two prices. Take a 105 call on a $100 stock, thirty days out, genuinely worth 1.662 at 30 volatility. Quote it two cents wide and the implied volatility runs from 29.90% to 30.10% — a fifth of a point, fine. Quote it ten cents wide, which is unremarkable on a single name, and the band is 29.51% to 30.49% : a 0.98 volatility point range, and the column shows you one number from inside it. Twenty cents wide and it is nearly two points. So the practical rule is that an IV column is only as precise as the spread it was computed from, and comparing two names' implieds to a decimal place is usually comparing their liquidity. Page 14 takes this much further — on a short-dated wing a single tick can be eleven volatility points. Volume and open interest answer different questions and get confused constantly. Volume is what traded today; open interest is what is still outstanding. A strike with enormous volume and no open interest was traded and closed — somebody was in and out. Enormous open interest and no volume is a position somebody is sitting on, and it is the one that matters for pinning. The mid is not a price. It is the average of two prices, one of which you can hit and one of which you can lift, and on a wide market it is a number nobody will trade. Every apparent edge under about half a spread is an artifact of quoting the mid. The volatility band a quote actually implies Controls Notice the band widens sharply out in the wings even at constant quote width. The same ten cents is a fifth of a point at the money and several points on a far strike, because vega collapses faster than the spread does.

chapters.title: Skew and term structure, read by eye
chapters.dek: Two shapes on a screen, both readable in a glance once you know what you are looking for.

figures.title: The two shapes: skew down a column, term structure across them
figures.caption: Notice the lower panel. A hump at the front is an event; a smooth rise is a market that expects more volatility later; a smooth fall is one that expects less. Three shapes, three completely different trades.

checks.q: The front week shows 82% implied and the six-month shows 30%. What is that?
checks.right: Almost certainly a scheduled event inside the front week. A fixed event contributes a fixed variance, and dividing it by a very short T makes the annualized number enormous
checks.why: A date, not a mispricing. The giveaway is the size and the shape: an 82% front against a 30% back is far too large to be an opinion about ordinary volatility and far too neat to be an error. Before ever concluding that a front month is expensive, find out what is in it — earnings, an FDA decision, an index reconstitution — because the arithmetic that makes it look expensive is the arithmetic of dividing by a small number.

terms.Risk reversal: The 25-delta put's implied volatility minus the 25-delta call's. A single number for how much more the downside costs than the upside, and the way skew is quoted between desks.
terms.Normalized skew: Wing implied vol divided by at-the-money implied vol, minus one. It measures skew as a percentage of the vol level, so that names and regimes with different vol can be compared.

chapters.text: Scan the IV column downward. If the numbers fall as the strike rises, the column is skewed, and how fast they fall is how skewed. On the example chain here — thirty days, 28% at the money — the 90 strike shows 32.10% and the 110 shows 24.99% , so the column drops seven volatility points across four strikes. The standard way to compress that into one number is the risk reversal : the 25-delta put's implied minus the 25-delta call's. On this surface it is 3.77 points at thirty days, 6.47 at ninety and 12.29 at a year, because a skew defined in log-moneyness reaches further out as the strikes spread. Points are the wrong unit for comparing names, or one name across regimes. Seven points of skew on a 28-vol stock and seven points on a 70-vol stock are not the same steepness. Divide instead: the 90 strike's 32.10% over the 100 strike's 28.12% is 1.142, so the downside trades at a 14.2% premium , and the 110 strike at an 11.1% discount. That ratio is normalized skew , and it is the one to rank on. Read it against three things before calling it steep: the vol level, since wing vols move less than at-the-money vol and the ratio therefore compresses when vol is high and stretches when it is low; the name's own history; and what the rest of the market is doing that day. Now scan across expiries instead, at the money. A flat term structure is a stock with nothing scheduled. A front month standing well above the back is the screen telling you a date exists — and the size of the step says what the market has priced for it. With a 28% baseline and one event worth a 7% move, the quoted at-the-money runs 82.1% at three days, 57.8% at a week, 37.2% at a month and 29.7% at six months. The event has not moved; its share of the remaining variance has. Page 08 is that arithmetic in full. The two shapes: skew down a column, term structure across them Controls Notice the lower panel. A hump at the front is an event; a smooth rise is a market that expects more volatility later; a smooth fall is one that expects less. Three shapes, three completely different trades. Try this Put an event worth 7% into the term structure and predict what the three-day implied does before you look. Most people guess about 40%.

chapters.title: Before you believe the IV column, find the forward
chapters.dek: Every implied vol on a screen was computed from a forward price somebody assumed. If the assumption is wrong, so is the whole column.

figures.title: One market, two IV columns
figures.caption: The two columns open like scissors, and each blade is furthest from the truth on its in-the-money side. Where the call line stops, the call is quoted below what the screen thinks is its minimum value, and no volatility can explain it.

checks.q: A screen shows put implied vols well above call implied vols at every strike, by a similar amount. The first thing to conclude is:
checks.right: The screen's forward is too high: a borrow cost or dividend it does not know about
checks.why: The forward is too high. Skew is a difference across strikes; this is a difference between calls and puts at the same strike, which parity does not allow. The only free parameter is the forward. Selling the "rich" puts against the calls is a reversal, and what you would collect is exactly the borrow you then pay.

chapters.text: Here is a ninety-day chain on a stock that costs 6% a year to borrow. The screen does not know that. It backs each implied vol out of the option's price using the interest rate alone, and plots calls and puts separately. Both lines come from the same market, in which a call and a put at one strike have the same volatility. One market, two IV columns Carry The two columns open like scissors, and each blade is furthest from the truth on its in-the-money side. Where the call line stops, the call is quoted below what the screen thinks is its minimum value, and no volatility can explain it. At the 100 strike the calls say 23.8% and the puts say 31.3%. The market is trading 27.8%. Nothing is mispriced: the screen believes the forward is 100.99 and the options are priced off 99.51, and that $1.48 lands in the call as cheapness and in the put as richness. The forward is on the screen if you look for it. Take any strike near the money and use parity: [equation: F = K + (C − P) × e^rT] Reads as: the forward is the strike plus the call-minus-put, grown at the interest rate to expiry. Here 100 + (5.201 − 5.688) × 1.0099 = 99.51, and a forward that far below spot-plus-interest is a 6% borrow. So the order is fixed. Forward first, from call-minus-put at one or two strikes around the money. Then the implied vols, using that forward. Only then the shape. A screen that skips the first step shows you carry and calls it skew. And when you cannot fix the forward, lean on the out-of-the-money side. A forward error moves an option's price by its delta, so the deep in-the-money option, with a delta near one, absorbs nearly all of it. At the 115 strike the out-of-the-money call reads 21.7% against a true 23.5%, off by 1.8 points; the in-the-money put reads 32.9%, off by 9.4. Try this Tell the screen about the borrow. Predict what the two lines do when its assumed carry matches the market's.

chapters.title: The five-second scan
chapters.dek: A procedure, in order. It is short because the point is that it fits in the time before somebody expects an answer.

figures.title: A live chain, with the conversions already done
figures.caption: Notice how few rows are actually in play. On a typical monthly chain the body and shoulders are five or six strikes; everything else is a wing, and wings are where the spread is widest and the implied least reliable.

checks.q: Why does the scan start with the sigma rather than with the prices?
checks.right: Because until you have it, no strike distance on the screen means anything — every later judgement is relative to that one number
checks.why: It is the unit everything else is measured in. Reading prices before you know the scale is like reading a map with no key: you can see that one number is bigger than another and you cannot tell whether the difference matters. It is also the cheapest step — one multiplication — which is why it goes first.

chapters.text: Everything above is a conversion. This is the order to do them in, and it is worth doing in the same order every time until it stops being a list and becomes a glance. Zero — check that calls and puts agree. If the two IV columns differ at the same strike, the screen has the wrong forward. Fix that first, as in chapter 06; nothing below means anything until they agree. One — get the sigma. Spot times the at-the-money implied times √T. One number, and every strike distance on the screen is now readable. On the chain below it is printed at the top of the panel, and after a hundred chains you will be computing it before the page has finished loading. Two — locate the money. Not the 50-delta; the strike nearest the forward . On short-dated equity chains they are nearly the same, and on anything long-dated or high-carry they are not. Three — read the shape of the IV column. Not the values, the slope. Falling as strikes rise is ordinary equity skew. Falling then rising is a smile, which means the wings are bid on both sides and usually means jump risk. Flat is either an index in a calm week or a screen showing you a model rather than a market. Four — check the front against the back. One step at the front is an event. A smooth slope is a view. Five — look at the spreads before believing any of it. Everything in steps one to four was computed from mids. The chain below tags every strike as body, shoulder or wing by its distance in sigmas, which is the classification the scan is really producing. It is not standard terminology; the distinction it draws is completely standard. A live chain, with the conversions already done Controls Notice how few rows are actually in play. On a typical monthly chain the body and shoulders are five or six strikes; everything else is a wing, and wings are where the spread is widest and the implied least reliable. Try this Cut the expiry to three days without changing anything else, and count how many strikes are left that are not wings.

chapters.title: Drill the conversions
chapters.dek: Sigmas, strike distances and deltas, at the speed the screen moves.

figures.caption: Tolerances are loose enough for mental arithmetic and tight enough that guessing fails. Estimating is the skill; the calculator is not on the desk when someone asks.

checks.q: A $100 stock at 30 volatility, thirty days out. How big is a one-sigma move?
checks.why: $8.60, and the third answer is the interesting wrong one. Dividing the volatility by twelve rather than by √12 is the single most common units error in the subject. Time enters through its square root, always — a month is 0.287 of a year in volatility terms, not 0.083.

checks.q: Same stock and expiry, five-point strikes. How many strikes fit inside one standard deviation?
checks.right: About 1.7 — $8.60 of sigma divided by $5 of spacing
checks.why: 1.7 strikes per sigma. The third answer inverts it, which is worth doing deliberately once: 0.58 is the number of sigmas per strike , and both quantities are useful as long as you know which one you are holding.

checks.q: How good is "the 16-delta is the one-sigma strike"?
checks.right: Good to about a tenth of a sigma inside three months — 1.06 at a week, 1.13 at a month, 1.24 at a quarter — and it degrades to 1.56 at a year
checks.why: A short-dated rule, and the put side is not its mirror. The 16-delta put runs 0.94, 0.88, 0.80 and 0.64 sigma over the same tenors — moving the opposite way. The asymmetry is the lognormal, and it is why a delta-defined strangle is not centered on the spot.

checks.q: A 105 call worth 1.66 is quoted ten cents wide. What is the implied volatility?
checks.right: Somewhere between 29.51% and 30.49%. The quote is a band nearly a full volatility point wide, and the column shows one number from inside it
checks.why: A band, not a number. Ten cents is unremarkable on a single name and it is already a point of volatility. Comparing two screens' implieds to a decimal place, without their spreads beside them, is usually comparing their liquidity.

checks.q: The front week is 82% implied and the six-month is 30%. What is the most likely explanation?
checks.right: A scheduled event inside the front week. A fixed event variance divided by a very short T produces an enormous annualized number
checks.why: A date. With a 28% baseline and one event worth a 7% move, the quoted at-the-money runs 82.1% at three days and 29.7% at six months — the event has not changed, only its share of the remaining variance. Find out what is scheduled before calling anything expensive.

checks.q: A strike shows enormous open interest and almost no volume today. What does that tell you?
checks.right: Somebody is sitting on a position there. Volume is what traded today; open interest is what is still outstanding — and it is the one that matters for pinning into expiry
checks.why: An existing position, not today's activity. The third answer describes the opposite pattern — big volume with no open interest is somebody in and out. The two columns answer different questions and the confusion between them is common enough to be worth a deliberate check: today , or outstanding ?
